newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss bank compensates Czech family for lost funds.
newsitem.headline: Swiss bank compensates Czech family for lost funds.

text.p: One of Switzerland's biggest banks said on Sunday it had offered to compensate a Czech family of Holocaust survivors whose Swiss bank account was mysteriously closed in 1941 without their approval.

Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) said its review of the case, unearthed by a Swiss newspaper, found it was impossible to determine now what happened to the money, but that it was ready to offer compensation as a gesture of good will.

UBS spokeswoman Gertrud Erismann said the bank was prepared to do the same thing in other cases if former wartime account holders could make a solid case that the wealth they deposited for safekeeping from Hitler had vanished without a trace.
"We will take a serious look and if we have the feeling it is a case where one should make a gesture, then we will naturally do so," she told Reuters.
The case highlights controversy over Jewish groups' claims that Swiss banks are sitting on billions of dollars in unclaimed wealth from Holocaust victims.

Banks deny this, but are working with Jewish groups to comb their books for any dormant accounts that may have escaped two previous sweeps for such funds. Big banks also helped finance a memorial fund for Holocaust victims as a sign of good will.

The SonntagsZeitung weekly reported that Josef Blum, a Czech Jew and vodka distiller, came to Zurich in May 1938 to convert his standard account at UBS into a depository account in his own name and that of his two children, Heinz and Luise.

To prevent UBS from paying out funds on instructions drawn up under duress -- as the Nazis forced many Jews to do -- the shrewd businessman agreed a code so that UBS would only transfer money if a withdrawal request had a "B." under the signature.
He gave UBS a cheque for $14,785.20 to buy U.S. Treasury bonds and American Telephone and Telegraph (AT&T) bonds, then returned to Czechoslovakia, where he died only 13 days later.

Luise, then 19, and 16-year-old Heinz watched in horror as Nazi Germany annexed the Sudentenland later that year and swallowed the rest of the country in 1939. But their plan to emigrate failed when Germans sealed the borders, the paper said.

Nazi thugs who arrested Luise's husband in 1940 and searched her apartment failed to find her father's bank documents, but -- panicked they might be found in the next search -- she copied the details into a cookbook and destroyed the original papers.

Swept up in the Nazis' plan to exterminate Europe's Jews, Luise and Heinz were shipped off to the Theresienstadt concentration camp in 1942, the paper said, quoting Heinz's widow, Vera Blum, who now lives in Israel.
Heinz was transferred to a labour camp in 1944. Luise was sent to Auschwitz -- where her husband was murdered -- then to Bergen-Belsen and back to Theresienstadt.
Both siblings survived, and set out on a decades-long effort to recover the money their father had deposited in Switzerland.

Luise discovered the old cookbook by chance in 1971, helping Heinz, who then lived in Israel, track down wealth their father had deposited in Palestine before the war. But the search in Switzerland ran into a stone wall.

At first UBS said it could find no record of Josef Blum's deposit number 21 300 from 1938, then said later the account had existed but was closed before the end of 1941. It had destroyed all the relevant records on who got the money after 10 years.
Outraged, the family hired a lawyer to press their argument that no one could have withdrawn the money in 1941 because Josef Blum was dead and his children were trapped in Czechoslovakia.
They ruled out the possibility that ultra-cautious Blum could have given anyone else power of attorney, but dropped the case because they could not afford to bring a suit against UBS.
The Blum case came to light again only when journalist Beat Balzli came across it while researching Switzerland's role as a wartime financial centre with close ties to Nazi Germany.
"We looked at all the documents that are available today and decided that...you cannot with certainty exclude the possibility that something went wrong. Where, we don't know," Erismann said.
"We have no idea if we made a mistake or if someone who was not authorised withdrew the money. It is one of those cases where we now have to make a gesture, and that is why we offered a settlement."

Erismann declined to say how large the offer was, adding it was still under discussion with the Blum family. She said she did not believe it was the first time UBS had offered such compensation, but did not elaborate.
